title: Chapter 49 – Hollow Echo
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

The gate Warden teaches by hitting things.

It does not speak, and it does not gesture. It stands at the foot of the black stone steps with its granite shield on its arm and its amber lamp turned toward the boy, and when Jian has been standing in front of it for a quarter of an hour, wondering what it wants, it lifts one vast hand and brings it down on the nearest boulder.

The boulder does not break. It rings.

It is a low, round, sweet note, like a finger drawn round the rim of a bowl, and it goes on much longer than it should. Jian feels it in his chest. It runs out across the moss and into the beds, and from somewhere beyond the pool comes a faint return, a second note, a quarter-tone flatter, and then a third, until the whole hollow of the Orchard is humming softly with the memory of one blow.

It says this is the way, says Pebble, from his shoulder. It says you must hit the empty place.

"Which empty place?"

Every thing has one, she translates, a little doubtfully. It says. Inside the thing. The place where the thing is not.

He looks at the boulder. It is a block of gray granite the size of a sleeping cow, and as far as he can tell it is solid all through. Then he thinks of the cart wheel at the Narrows, the hollow hub, the seam in the Qi shell below an armpit. He thinks that he has spent two months looking at the gap in things.

"It means the seam," he says slowly.

Yes. Pebble sounds relieved. It says you are not stupid, only small.

* * *

The stele is behind the steps.

He has passed it a dozen times without seeing it, because it is the color of the stone and the moss has grown over its lower half. It is a plain slab of black basalt, taller than a man, set upright in a bed of white pebbles. When the gate Warden lays a single twig-finger against it, a pattern of faint silver lines wakes across the face, a spiral, like the whorl of a shell, with a tiny figure at its center.

The figure is a man. He is kneeling. He has his hands pressed flat against the ground, and from his mouth, in a series of thin curved lines, a sound is leaving him and traveling outward, ring on ring, through the earth.

Under it, in an old, spare, upright hand, three characters.

```
[ARK-7 — SCAN]
Object: Orchard stele (manual art, inscribed).
Technique: HOLLOW ECHO.
Grade: Yellow, high tier. Requires: Qi Refining 7+.
Effect: Sends a pulse of Qi into a solid; the pulse returns
from every cavity, seam or flaw within its range.
Secondary: A struck hollow vessel may be shattered.
Range: 8th stage — approx. 90 paces through stone.
Cost: RECOIL. One-tenth of each pulse returns to the caster
as a blow to the dantian. Pulse is audible to any
seam-sensitive creature within 300 paces.
Note: Technique teaches 'listening to what is absent.'
```

Recoil, he thinks. And a bell. Of course. It is the interface's whole philosophy, in four words: every advantage has a cost, and the cost is generally in the same place as the advantage.

He reads it twice. Then he sits down in the moss at the foot of the stele, with his legs crossed and Pebble in his lap, and begins to learn.

* * *

It takes him nine days.

For the first three he does nothing but listen. He sits with his palms on the ground and his eyes shut and lets the Orchard speak, a long soft slow murmur of root and water and stone, until he can tell the weight of a bed by the pitch of its hum. The Wardens bring him water in a bronze cup. Limp, the lame one, brings him a flat bun of some bitter gray meal that tastes of sawdust and makes him feel, for an hour afterward, as if he has been rinsed. He does not ask where it comes from.

On the fourth day he sends his first pulse.

It is a small one. He gathers a thread of Qi in his palm, and lets it leave him through the moss, and listens. For one long moment there is nothing. Then, from forty paces to the east, a faint cold answer comes back, a hollow tock, and a picture forms in his mind with perfect clarity: a space under the ground, a crack, the long root of a Warden's foot running through it like a vein.

And then the recoil hits.

It is not a large thing. It is a small hard fist, driven into the pit of his stomach from the inside. His breath goes out of him in a whoosh. His eyes water. For a count of five he cannot think.

Ow, says Pebble, with feeling. I felt that.

"Yes. I thought you might."

You should do it again. She sounds quite bright. It was a good one.

He does it again. The fist is a little harder. He does it a third time, and a fourth, and by the sixth pulse he has stopped feeling anything but a faint cold sickness under the ribs and the whisper of Pebble's voice, which is pleased, as a small child is pleased by a loud noise. He stops at nine. He lies on the moss with his hands on his belly and his eyes on the pearly roof, and does not move for an hour.

That, he thinks, is why they teach it in a garden. A man who learned this in a battle would be dead by the third pulse. The Orchard air gives him back, each time, a little of what the blow has taken. He is learning in the only place in the world where the lesson is affordable.

I will not be able to use it outside. Not more than twice.

Not more than twice, Pebble agrees, rolling onto her back. Maybe once. And then everyone with a nose will know where you are.

* * *

On the fifth day he finds the Orchard's other hollow.

He is not looking for it. He has been practicing on the far wall, a sheet of white stone that rings like a plate, and he sends a pulse down through the floor instead of across, because he is tired and his aim has wandered. It goes into the earth. It goes a long way.

It does not come back.

He waits. A count of ten. A count of twenty. He has braced for the fist, and it does not arrive, and a cold prickle runs up his spine as he understands what that means.

The pulse has not hit anything.

He sends a second. Stronger. He puts his whole reserve behind it, a thread as thick as his finger, and pours it into the ground at the foot of the stele.

This time something answers.

It is very far down. Fifty paces. Seventy. Ninety, at the very edge of his range, where the thread is already thin as spider silk. A single, huge, hollow note, deep as a church bell, rising out of the dark like a bubble out of a pond. It comes up through the stone and rings in his bones. And then the fist hits, and it is not a fist. It is a hammer, and he goes over on his side with a gasp and lies in the moss with his hands over his ears.

Pebble is on his chest. She is trembling all over.

Cold place, she whispers. Cold, cold, cold. Big. Under. It heard.

"Heard what?"

You.

He lies very still. It is a strange feeling, being listened to by a hill. The Orchard hums around him, soft and unalarmed. The Wardens stand in their ring. And far below them, so deep that his mind can barely hold the number, something very large and very old has turned over in its sleep, once, and gone back to dreaming.

```
[ARK-7 — NOTICE]
Hollow Echo: detected resonance at ~90 paces below.
Structure: large enclosed void (est. 40 x 20 x 12 paces).
Seam-adjacent. Not a natural cavity.
Level 2 Scan: insufficient. Recommend: Level 3.
```

A room, he thinks. A big room, under the Orchard, under the hill.

He thinks of Mu, forty miles away, with his lilies and his patience. He thinks of the old woman Mei Ru spoke of, who reads the hill with knucklebones, and who will have heard the same hush in the vein that he has just heard in the stone. Something under the hill is awake, and I have just told it where I am. The thought is cold and exact. It does not make him feel better that the thing has gone back to sleep.

Under the pool, says the small cold part of him, with great tidiness, remembering what Mei Ru said, with her last breath, in the green light. Everything they want is under a pool.

He does not move. He does not try again. He has no intention, ever, of trying again from here.

* * *

On the tenth day Hu bursts into the granary and shouts at the sky.

It is a very good shout. It starts low and climbs, in a long ragged roll, and the crows on the roof take off in a black cloud. Jian, who is sitting on an upturned crate in the corner with a half-copied sheet of drawing paper, flinches and drops his brush.

"Heartroot," says Hu.

He is standing in the middle of the floor with his one arm up and the bent rod clenched in his fist. His hair is wild. His one good eye is blazing. He has not had a drink in sixty days, and has, in that time, put on a few pounds and lost a great deal of his stoop, and now, in the afternoon light, with a slip of yellow paper in his hand, he looks for all the world like a man who has seen his own ghost and found it wearing his face.

"Who gave you Heartroot?" says Hu. "I ask politely. Who. Gave. You. Heartroot."

"Hu—"

"Don't. Don't say Hu. Don't say a word until I have finished." He flings the slip onto the table. It lands among the clay bottles, a thin sheet of old, brown, brittle paper, covered in a cramped hand. It is one of two old slips Jian took from Mei Ru's belt before he burned her, and has carried since, wrapped in a handkerchief, and handed to Hu three weeks ago as scrolls from the ruin lot. "I read this on the day you gave it to me. Tally's slips I knew, every one. This. This I did not know. It says heartroot leaf, fresh, one. It says Grade Three, high tier. It says Heartroot pill, for the mending of cracked cores. And it is missing the last line."

"I know," says Jian.

"I looked at it for a week." Hu is shaking. "I thought, this is a recipe for a pill that I could never brew. Heartroot is ten stones the leaf. The Pavilion sells a sack a year, to the Sect. I thought, it is a rich man's thing. I put it in my pocket." He lifts his one hand, spread, in the air, like a man about to pray. "And this morning I find this on my table."

He pushes aside a bottle. Beneath it, on a square of white cloth, lies a single silver-gray leaf, as long as his hand, with a faint dew on its veins.

"It is fresh," says Hu hoarsely. "It was plucked this morning. I know the smell. I have not smelled it since I was twenty-five, in the Sect's own stillroom. Where did you get it?"

Jian opens his mouth. He closes it. He has thought about this moment for three weeks, and every sentence he has prepared has been a lie.

"Mother brought it," he says. "She has a source. She would not say."

It is not a lie. It is the least of the truths. He holds Hu's eye, steadily, and feels something in his chest shift, like a stone settling.

Hu stares at him. For a very long moment he does not speak. His mouth works.

"A source," he says at last.

"Yes."

"A source who sells one leaf of Heartroot, fresh, on a day when there is no frost, to a woman who is married to the Patriarch of a poor clan with a dying vein." The old man's voice is dry as paper. "That is a very interesting source."

"Hu."

"I am not asking." He lowers the hand. He looks, suddenly, very tired. "I told you once, in the spring, that I have been asked nothing by better men. I will go on to say that I do not intend to ask, now. It is a courtesy. I know what a courtesy costs." He looks at the leaf, and at the boy, and at the roof. "But I should like it understood that I am a man of one eye and one arm, and I am not blind."

"I know."

"I shall say nothing."

"Thank you."

"I shall merely brew," says Hu, with something close to a smile, "like an honest fool."

* * *

They brew it in the dead of the night, with the shutters closed and a lamp turned low.

It is Mother's hands and Hu's furnace. Hu cannot lift the pot with one arm, and Qinghe cannot read the old forge notation, and between them, as the small iron kettle sings on the coals, they pass the work back and forth in a silence that is almost a conversation. He measures. She stirs. She says now, and he says not yet, and she says Hu, very gently, and he says very well. Once, near midnight, he laughs aloud, a startled shout, and says that he has never in his life seen a woman handle a Grade Three so lightly, and Qinghe says, calmly, that she has handled a great many things lightly that were not.

Jian sits in the corner, with Pebble in his lap, and watches.

It is not the pill that he is watching for. It is the other thing.

On the table, beside the pot, lies the other slip from Mei Ru's belt. It is the older of the two, and the more worn. It is not a Grade Three, or a talisman, or a pill. It is a scrap of paper no longer than a man's hand, crimped at the edge, with a half-burned corner and a single faded line of text.

Nine Turn pill. Peak tier. Grade Five.

Ninefold marrow vine, one. Moon-ash lotus, one.

Heartroot, three.

Frostbell, seven.

Mourner's cup, nine. And then, in the same hand, but lighter, as if the writer had wished to deny it: A man who takes this should expect to live.

He has read it, he thinks, four hundred times.

Heartroot, frostbell, mourner's cup. The Orchard has all three. It has, he is almost sure, forty of each. But there are two herbs on that list that he has not found, in nine days of walking the beds, and the interface, when he asked, gave him only a flat answer.

```
[ARK-7 — NOTICE]
Recipe: NINE TURN PILL. Grade 5, peak tier. INCOMPLETE.
Missing reagents: Ninefold marrow vine; Moon-ash lotus.
Orchard inventory: 0 of 2. Search progress: 31/31 species
surveyed in current zone.
Note: Remaining herbs may exist in other zones, or outside.
```

Outside, thinks Jian. Somewhere.

A sound pulls him back. Hu has dropped the stirring rod. It is ringing on the stone floor, and the old man is standing with his one hand pressed to his mouth, and a thick golden steam is rolling up out of the pot in a slow, smooth, intoxicating cloud, and every one of the little clay bottles on the table has begun, very faintly, to hum.

"Oh," says Hu, in a whisper. "Oh, you dear thing. Look at it."

"It is done," says Qinghe.

It is. At the bottom of the little iron pot, in a pool of clear liquid, lies a single pill, no larger than a pea, the color of old honey. It glows. It gives off a warmth that Jian can feel from across the room. She lifts it out on a bone spoon with a hand that is not quite steady, and drops it into a jar of white clay, and for a long moment nobody says anything at all.

"Grade Three," says Hu, finally. "A high. I have not seen the like since the Veiled Forge fell. And it is the first of ten." His voice breaks. "The first of ten."

* * *

The Stone Skin talisman is harder, and it is Wenyuan's.

He draws it in the study, in the dark of the moon, with the door barred and a towel stuffed under it. Jian sits on the floor with his back to the wall and watches. It is the only way he has ever learned anything, and he has learned, in two years, that his father draws the way other men breathe.

The ink is the first difficulty. The slip says Heartroot sap, a thimble, warm. It says gray-bark resin, from a stone that has been taught to stand. It does not say where a man finds such a thing. Jian has found it. Limp shed a strip of its own bark on the fourth morning, a long gray curl as thick as a thumb, and when he picked it up it was heavy and warm and smelled of rain on a hot roof. He has not asked what a Warden's bark costs the Warden. He has put it, with some shame, in a small clay pot, and carried it here.

"Resin," says Wenyuan. He rolls it between finger and thumb. "It is alive. It is a living thing. It ought not to hold a stroke at all."

"It will."

"I am quite sure it will. I am merely observing that it is a very strange pen." The Patriarch dips the brush. His hand is steady. His face is calm and slightly absent, the face of a man listening to music in another room. "Stone Skin. Yellow grade, high tier. It turns the body to granite for twenty breaths. It will stop a sword, but not a drum. It makes a man heavy. If he is a fool, he will sink in a pond."

He draws.

It is not a thing the eye can follow. The brush goes down, and comes up, and goes down. A line, a hook, a long soft curve. The characters rise on the yellow paper like frost forming on a window. Each stroke glows a faint, steady gray as it is laid, and the glow does not fade. It sinks. It goes into the paper, into the fibers, until the whole sheet is the dull color of river stone, and a thin hum fills the room.

It takes him forty-one breaths. At the end he sets the brush down, and for a moment he does not move.

"Father?"

"I am fine." The voice is thin. "I am only observing that I have spent a month's Qi on one sheet. At the old rate, I should have drawn three. And that if I draw two more, I shall lie on the floor for the rest of the night." He opens his eyes. The talisman lies before him, gray and cold and perfect. "It will stop a sword. I have no doubt of it. And it will cost the clan the better part of a day's work, from the one man who does it best, every time."

"Then you should not draw many."

"I should not draw one, if I were wise. A Stone Skin of this grade will sell in the Ford for forty stones." A pale ghost of a smile. "But I find, tonight, that I have a great many guards."

He holds it out.

Jian does not take it at once. He looks at it, at the soft gray lines, at his father's tired hand beneath it. It is a strange small thing to carry, a single sheet of paper, with a day of a man's life in it.

Everything has a cost, he thinks. Even the good things. Especially the good things.

"Thank you," he says, and takes it.

* * *

He gives the first one to Wenshi.

It is Mother's idea, and Wenyuan's. The Patriarch's brother has not slept through a night since the Narrows. His wrist, which was broken in the rockfall, has set badly. Something has gone wrong in the bone, and with it the arm's old strength, and a thing in him that has gone wrong with it is quieter and worse. He has stopped drilling the guard. He has stopped speaking in council. He sits in the guardhouse, in Mao's old chair, and cleans the same sword.

Jian brings it to him himself, on a plain tray, at dusk.

"What's this?" says Wenshi.

"Medicine. Mother made it."

"I don't want medicine." His voice is flat. He does not look up from the blade. "I want the arm I had. If you can bring me that, you can bring it. Otherwise, boy, put it down and go to bed."

Jian puts down the tray. He does not go.

After a long time, Wenshi sets down the sword and picks up the pill. He looks at it, a small round golden bead, in the dim. A faint warmth is already coming off it, into his rough palm.

"What is it?"

"Heartroot."

"Don't be an idiot. Heartroot's the Pavilion's. We couldn't afford it if we sold the hall."

"No. We couldn't."

The big man's head comes up. His eyes, red-rimmed, sunk in his gaunt face, travel over the boy. Something moves behind them. It is not hope; he is not a man who has room for it. It is something older and fiercer. It is a kind of stubborn, wary respect.

"You'll tell me where it comes from," says Wenshi.

"No."

"Why not?"

"Because it would cost you something, and I don't yet know what." Jian meets his gaze. "I will tell you when I can."

Wenshi looks at him for a long, long time.

Then, abruptly, with no more ceremony than a man swallowing a nail, he puts the pill in his mouth, and swallows it dry.

For a moment nothing happens. Then his whole body goes rigid. His jaw clenches. The knuckles of his left hand, whole and ruined, go white on the arm of the chair. A groan comes up out of him, long and low, and under it the faint sound, like the creak of a ship's timbers, of something very old settling back into its place.

When it is over, he is sitting very still. A film of sweat has broken out along his brow. He lifts his right hand, the splinted one, and slowly, carefully, makes a fist.

"Oh," says Wenshi. His voice is hoarse. "Oh, Mao."

Jian does not say anything. He stands in the doorway, in the gathering dusk, with Pebble warm against his throat and the thrum of a ninety-pace hollow still in the back of his mind, a note he cannot forget. Behind the wall, in the courtyard, a few of the guards are laughing at something. The sound is ordinary and warm.

The first of ten, he thinks. And somewhere under the Orchard, a room that heard me.

He does not know which of the two will cost more.
